Since Nf6 or Nb6 would leave black without enough pressure in the center, Nb4 misplaces the knight only to create the obvious threat of Qxd4 followed by Nc2, Nxc3 is forced. Although d4 is strengthened, the queenside weakens, and the a1-h8 diagonal loosens up.  That is why g6 and Bg7 is played in the Gruenfeld Defence. Black will now play to dismantle white's central ambitions. Usually, Black advances the c-pawn, and then he uses his e-pawn to dismantle white's center. Also, Nb4?? loses to Qa4+ Nc6 d5.
After e4, White has a dangerous center. Black must pressure it or risk a cramped, passive game. The only good move is Nxc3, else play resembles the dubious Marshall defence.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3n4/N2P4/8/PP2PPPP.text: This strange looking move was first employed by Ashot Nadanian in 1996. Usually it is not recommended to put Knights on the edge of the board, but here it is meaningful. White takes the important c5-square under control and is going to force black's Knight from the center with е4. Eventually, the a4-Knight can occupy the c5-square and attack the pawn on b7.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/n1p2n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P.text:
Black develops the knight to a6 in order to later transfer it to b4, which was weakened by White's move 5. a4. This does however give White time to occupy the center with 6. e4, or to support the d-pawn with 6. e3.
Regardless of whether White pushes the e-pawn one or two squares, Black's response is going to be 6...Bg4, pinning the knight on f3 to the white queen. This is different from the Steiner variation, where the knight isn't actually pinned and can move to e5, gaining a tempo on the bishop.
After 6. e4 Bg4 7. Bxc4 it is possible for Black to play 7...Bxf3, doubling White's pawns since 8. Qxf3 would lose the d4 pawn. Despite being a pawn down, this position is still fine for White who can choose to create doubled pawns on Black's a-file with 9. Bxa6. A more modest approach is 7...e6, blunting White's light-squared bishop.

**History**
This opening is named after the Russian GM Vasily Smyslov. While not the first person to play this variation (the position was reached before in 1926), he popularized it in 1959. The move has lost its popularity over time, being mostly used as a surprise weapon.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/P1pP2b1/2N2N2/1.text:
Instead of the usual 5...Bf5, Black opts to put the bishop on g4, harassing White's knight. However, because the e-pawn hasn't advanced, the knight isn't actually pinned to the queen, so White can play 6. Ne5 with a tempo on the Bishop.
After the bishop retreats with 6...Bh5, White has the option to go for either 7. f3, preparing e4, or 7. g3, preparing to fianchetto.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N2N2/1.text:
Black develops their light-squared bishop. This is possible now because the threat of Qb3 is no longer present thanks to the pawn on c4.
White should try to regain their pawn, which can be done in two ways.
6. e3 is the Dutch variation. This is the classical main line. White tries to capture the pawn with 7. Bxc4 and continues the game by castling and preparing to play e4.
6. Ne5 is the central variation. Instead of recapturing the pawn with the bishop, White tries to do so with their knight instead. This is White's most ambitious option and leads to sharper positions.
6. Nh4, the Bled attack, is the chief sideline for White. Instead of going after the pawn, White first tries to get rid of Black's light-squared bishop. This move can be played in the Dutch variation too, and the positions may transpose into each other.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/2BP4/4PN2/PP3PP.text:
Black strikes back at the center, potentially leaving White with an isolated queen's pawn after ...cxd4.
White's main option is 6. O-O, getting their king out of the center.
An alternative is 6. Qe2, the Furman variation. This supports the advance of the e-pawn and enables dxc5 without trading the queens.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPPN3/8/PP3PPP/.text:
This move is Black's best option to fight for an advantage. It forces White to either gambit the d4 pawn for activity, or to retreat the knight back to c3, "losing" a tempo in the process.
6. Bd2 is the main move, blocking the check and attacking Black's bishop at the same time. This does however block the white queen from defending the d4 pawn, allowing 6...Qxd4, which gambits the pawn in exchange for quick development and active pieces.
6. Nc3 is the Forgotten variation, a sideline where White holds onto the d4 pawn, keeping material equal.
6. Nd2? is a mistake, since it contains all the drawbacks of 6. Bd2 (losing d4) and none of the advantages (getting a very active dark-squared bishop). To add insult to injury, it also hampers the development of White's queenside by locking up the c1 bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2.text:
This is a waiting move: Black is waiting for White to develop the light-squared bishop with 6. Bd3. Black does so in order to win some important tempi on White's bishop to make space for Black's light-squared bishop on b7. This is called the Meran variation.
White doesn't have to follow this plan however. White can play 6. Qc2, the Anti-Meran, to avoid this line and make Black's development of the light-squared bishop more difficult.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/2n5/PP3PPP/.text: This is forced, as Nb6 and Nf6 lost time, and Nb4 lost to Qa4+ Nc6 d5. Now, Black appears to have improved White's center, but weakened the long diagonal when Black plays Bg7. Black will play ...Bg7 and ...c5 soon after.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP3N/2N5/1P.text:
White immediately goes after Black's light-squared bishop. The usual response is 6...e6, opening up the dark-squared bishop and preparing to recapture with the e-pawn.
6...Bc8 has also been tried, retreating the bishop to its home-square and arguing that the knight on h4 is misplaced. In practice, Black scores poorly in this line.

**Plans for White**
White will generally win back the c4 pawn with the moves e3 and Bxc4, which also allow White to castle kingside.
If Black has captured the knight with the e6 pawn, there will be a hanging pawn on f5. This pawn can usually be targeted with a move like Qc2, forcing Black to defend it with g6 which weakens the dark squares around the king.
Another common plan is for White to try to play e4. Since Black has a pawn on f5, this is usually prepared with the move f3, planning to recapture with the pawn to gain a strong center.

**Plans for Black**
Because of the move 5. a4, Black can place the dark-squared bishop on the b4-square, where it can't be kicked out by pawns.
The c pawn is often pushed to c5 to undermine White's center.
When 6...Bc8 is played, Black has to deal with the problem of the light-squared bishop again. If Black decides to play e6, the bishop will be locked behind pawns once again. Therefore, Black usually plays e5 in order to keep the light-squared bishop open. …

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.text:
White places their knight into the center to recapture the pawn on c4 while leaving the diagonal for the dark-squared bishop open. There are two theoretical responses for Black.
6...Nbd7 is the main move, letting White take on c4 and preparing to either put the knight on b6 or to play e5.
6...e6 is the Wiesbaden variation. This line involves White attempting to gain a lot of initiative and Black preventing it by sacrificing a piece for three pawns, generally leading to an endgame where Black tries to march an army of pawns down the board.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.text:
White opens up the light-squared bishop in order to recapture the pawn on c4. In doing so, the movement of the dark-squared bishop is temporarily restricted in the hopes to open it up later with e4.
6...e6 is played almost every time, looking to develop the dark-squared bishop to the b4-square, which has been weakened by White's choice to prevent b5 with 5. a4.
6...Na6 is a rare sideline called the Lasker variation, where Black tries to place their knight on b4, instead of the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPPN3/8/PP1B1PP.text: This move blocks the check and attacks Black's bishop, but loses sight of the d4-pawn. 6...Qxd4 picks up the gambitted pawn and threatens the knight on e4.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1PN2.text:
Blackburne Variation
After the developing move 6. e3, Black has 3 choices:
-She can take advantage of the Bishop being on f4 instead of g5, which doesn’t pressure the d5 pawn, and play 6...c5 without fear of being forced into an IQP structure. However, this line is entry to the rabbit hole and leads to very complicated positions.
-6...Nbd7 is a more solid choice and avoids the complications of the main line. However, it allows 7. c5 resulting in white having a pleasant space advantage.
-6...b6 is the most solid way for Black to play, resulting in positions resembling the Tartokower Defense.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2NBPN2.text:
White intends to enter the Meran variation. However, Black gets the final say in this matter.
After 6...dxc4 Black has officially entered the Meran variation, forcing White to move the bishop again to recapture the pawn.
If Black doesn't want to play the theoretical Meran, they can avoid it with 6...Bd6.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN2.text:
White proceeds with normal development. Black now has two options.

Go into the classical variation with 6...Nbd7.
Go for either Lasker's defense or the Tartakower variation with 6...h6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/2P5/P4PPP/R.text: With this forced recapture White strengthens their center, but their queenside is weak.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.text: This is a simple developing move. White's only real follow-up is 7. Nxc4, keeping the knights in the center and recapturing the c4 pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.text:
Black prepares to develop their dark-squared bishop to b4 where it stands uncontested thanks to White's move 5. a4.
If White tries to recapture the c4 pawn immediately with 7. Nxc4?! Black can strike back 7...c5, putting pressure on White's centre and garnering an advantage in development.
The only move that preserves White's advantage is 7. f3, trying to play e4 on the next move. This threat cannot be stopped by Black, who has to play for piece activity, potentially sacrificing a piece to destroy White's centre.

**History**
The Wiesbaden variation is named after the 1929 World Championship match between Alekhine and Bogoljubov. Bogoljubov entered the line in games three and five which took place in Wiesbaden.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/n1p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.text:
This move has a similar idea to the Smyslov variation: to bring the knight to the outpost on b4. White can continue playing in their usual fashion: 7. Bxc4 Nb4 8. O-O e6 9. Qe2, after which White will be able to play e4 without any issues. 9. Ne5 transposes to a line that can be reached from the Krause attack with 6...Na6, as can be seen in Carlsen - Vladimir, 2008.

**History**
This move was first played by, and named after, Emanuel Lasker in a game against Boris Verlinsky in 1925.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.text:
Black prepares to develop the dark-squared bishop to the b4-square, which was weakened by White's move 5. a4.
White can now simply recapture the c-pawn with 7. Bxc4.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPqN3/8/PP1B1PP.text: Black takes the gambitted pawn and will be up material for the time being. This opening doesn't come without compensation for White. After 7. Bxb4 White will have dominance over Black's weakened dark squares.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2pp4/2PP1B2/2N1PN2.text:
6...c5
Black immediately strikes the White centre with ...c7-c5. This takes advantage of the Bishop being on f4 instead of g5, which applies less pressure on d5. To demonstrate, after 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Nf3 Be7 5. Bg5 O-O 6. e3 h6 7. Bh4, 7...c5 can be met with 8. Bxf6 Bxf6 9. cxd5 exd5 10. dxc5, and Black is left with a suboptimal isolated queen’s pawn structure.
White’s only move is the Botvinnik exchange: 7. dxc5, forcing the black bishop on e7 to waste a tempo. 7. cxd5 can be met with ...Nxd5, and 7. Bd3 or 7. Be2 can be met with ...dxc4, which all allow black to equalise comfortably.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/8/2pP4/2NBPN2/P.text:
Black captures the c4 pawn with a tempo on White's bishop, forcing White to move it again.
7. Bxc4 is the only sensible move.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/4pn1p/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN.text:
Black pushes the bishop away, likely intending to go for either the Tartakower or Lasker's defence.
Apart from White's main option 7. Bh4 they can also avoid these theoretical lines by playing 7. Bxf6.

r1bq1rk1/pppnbppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN2.text:
With this move Black enters the Classical variation. This is an older and well-studied variation that has stood the test of time, as it is still played to this day. Due to its age, White has developed many responses to it over time.

7. Rc1 is the main line, developing the rook to the to-be-opened c-file.
7. Qc2 is the Rubinstein attack. White develops the queen to watch over the b1-h7 diagonal.
7. cxd5 releases the tension from the center and transposes into an exchange variation.
7. Bd3 is the Botvinnik variation, in which Black gains a few tempi on White's bishop with 7...cxd5 and, later on, Nb6.

**History**
The classical variation has been played all the way back in the late 1800's and has been deployed by and against the likes of Capablanca, Lasker, Alekhine, Kasparov and many more.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2P5/P4PPP/R1.text: With this move, Black occupies the long diagonal with their bishop and prepares the vital break ...c5.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2.text:
White recaptures the c4 pawn.
Black can now choose to either enter the Carlsbad variation with 7...Qc7 or to transfer the knight to b6 with 7...Nb6.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N2P2/.text:
White doesn't capture the c4-pawn. Instead, they prepare 8. e4, which comes with tempo on Black's bishop. With the support of the f-pawn, Black can't stop e4 from being played, so they must find an advantage by different means.
7...Bb4 is the main line. This move removes the knight's defence from e4 and has the idea of sacrificing the light-squared bishop on e4 in exchange for three pawns.
7...c5 tries to disrupt White's centre. After 8. e4 both 8...cxd4 and 8...Bg6 have been tried, but results have generally been favourable for White. This variation was also played in games 3, 5 and 8 of the 2010 World Chess Championship.
Modern engines prefer the move 7...Bg6, but this is rarely played and usually transposes after 8. e4 c5.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/P1BP4/2N1PN2/.text:
White reclaims their lost pawn. Black should follow up with 7...Bb4, pinning White's knight and putting it on a square where it can't be kicked out by pawns.
7...Nbd7 is also possible, but will most likely transpose back into the main line.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1BPqN3/8/PP3PPP/.text: White takes Black's dark-squared bishop. White's dark-squared bishop is now placed on a very active diagonal, cutting through d6, e7 and f8. Black should play 7...Qxe4+ to not be down a piece.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2Pp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/.text:
7. dxc5
White captures the c-pawn with 7. dxc5, forcing the black bishop on e7 to waste a tempo with 7...Bxc5. Note that 7...dxc4 leads to a favorable endgame for white after 8. Bxc4 Qxd1+ 9. Rxd1, where white enjoys more active pieces.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/8/2BP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
White recaptures the pawn.
7...b5 is the most proper response, justifying the loss of control over the center by making the b7-square available for the light-squared bishop while gaining a tempo.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2P2N2/P4PPP/.text: This move starts a piece setup that has become increasingly popular since the 1980's. White moves their knight to an active place. The drawback is that the bishop will have to settle for the passive e2-square, else Bg4 would be strong.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/2BPP3/2P5/P4PPP/R.text: This move places the bishop on a good, active post. However, the drawback is that Nf3 will become unplayable, since Bg4! will put unbearable pressure on d4. It's either Be2/Nf3, Bc4/Ne2 or Bc4/Nf3/h3. In this setup, the bishop will be more active, while in the other setup, the knight will be so. That other setup has increasingly popular since the 1980's.

r3kb1r/ppqnpppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2P.text:
Black develops the queen to c7 in order to prepare e5. This will likely lead to the Carlsbad variation.
White's main response is 8. g3 preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop to f4 where it can put pressure on the knight after 8...e5 9. dxe5 Nxe5. This also prepares to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/PbpP4/2N2P2/1.text:
Black makes use of the weakened b4-square, pressuring the knight on c3 and gaining a bit more control over e4.
The main line continues with 8. e4, also known as the Sharp line. Black has to sacrifice their light-squared bishop for three pawns if they want to retain any winning chances.
8. Nxc4 is White's main alternative, avoiding many of the complications that ensue from 8. e4. The position branches out after Black castles.
8. Bg5 is a rare continuation that has lost it's popularity over time. Usually Black responds with 8...h6, which gives their light-squared bishop a nicer square to go to if e4 happens.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.text:
Black develops the bishop to its most natural square.
White should simply castle kingside 8. O-O to get out of the pin and start preparing e4.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1BP1q3/8/PP3PPP/.text:
Black recaptures the piece. This is the starting point of the Marshall gambit. White has two main ways of blocking the check, both leading to complex positions where White has to find a way to convert their lead in development into a tangible advantage. White should generally avoid trading pieces, especially queens, as any endgame will favour Black.
8. Be2 is the main line, blocking the check with the bishop. This leaves the g2-pawn undefended, but taking it would be unwise, since it allows White to develop even more quickly with Bf3, Ne2 and then Rg2 comes with tempo.
8 Ne2 is less popular, but still very often played. This leaves the c4-pawn undefended, but taking it is once again way too dangerous for Black because of Qd6!, infiltrating on the weakened dark squares. The main continuation in this line ends up restoring material equality.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/P.text:
7...Bxc5
Black recaptures the pawn. Now White can play the unambitious 8. cxd5 and saddle black with an isolani, or continue going down the rabbit hole with the mainline 8. Qc2, where the queen points towards the black kingside. It should be noted that 8. a3 transposes into the mainline.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1ppp/2p1pn2/1p6/2BP4/2N1PN2/.text:
Black expands on the queenside and makes the b7-square available for their bishop while gaining a tempo on White's bishop.
White should retreat the bishop, there are three viable options:
8. Bd3 is the main line, returning the bishop to the square it was originally positioned on. From this square, it supports the e4 pawn-push and glances at Black's kingside.
8. Be2 is a more passive option. It can't be attacked as easily on e2 as on d3, but its also not as active in the attack.
8. Bb3 is the most aggressive option, keeping the bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal. White can generate a lot of pressure on the e6 and f7 pawns, possibly sacrificing a knight for the initiative. This option is not guaranteed if Black knows the theory well, so Black can come out with a slight edge if they are well prepared.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/4p2p/3p4/2PPn2B/2N1PN2.text:
Black centralizes the knight, opening up an attack on White's dark-squared bishop.
The mainline continues by trading the dark-squared bishops and later the knights as well.

rnbq1rk1/p1p1bpp1/1p2pn1p/3p4/2PP3B/2N1P.text: 7...b6 enters the Tartakower defence, where Black hopes to develop the light-squared bishop. While it looks like Black intends to fianchetto the bishop, this isn't necessarily true. If White tries to blunt the a8-h1 diagonal immediately with 8. cxd5, Black will nonetheless be able to develop the bishop: 8. cxd5 Nxd5 9. Bxe7 Qxe7 10. Nxd5 exd5 = and Black can now put the bishop somewhere on the c8-h3 diagonal instead (usually going to e6).

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/3PP3/2P2N2/P4PPP.text: This move is the key pawn lever, taking advantage of the diagonal. Note that the long diagonal is weak. Without this lever, d4 would be indestructible and the Grünfeld defence would be unsound. White has four main moves, the most theoretical being 8. Rb1.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/2BPP3/2P5/P4PPP/.text: This pawn lever also tries to attack the center. Since the center is potentially opening, white is well advised to move his king out of danger with 8.Ne2 followed by O-O.

r3kb1r/ppqnpppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N3P1/1P.text: This move prepares to develop both bishops; the dark-squared bishop to f4 and the light-squared bishop to g2. This move doesn't deter Black from playing 8...e5 which has been prepared with Black's previous moves.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/PbpPP3/2N2P2/.text:
White takes over the centre, attacking Black's bishop and opening up an attack on the c4-pawn. Retreating the bishop would be a mistake, since this gives White the full centre without any compensation.
Sacrificing the knight with 8...Nxe4? doesn't work, since after 9. fxe4 Qh4+ White can move their king to safety on the kingside. If 9. fxe4 Bxe4 Black doesn't have any pressure on the c3-knight, so 10. Be3 keeps everything held.
Thus, 8...Bxe4! is the main move to not have a passive position. White doesn't have much better than 9. fxe4, after which 9...Nxe4 threatens 10...Nxc3 11. bxc3 Bxc3+ 12. Bd2 Qxd4 to pick up a fifth pawn for the piece. White has two options in this position.

**Entering the endgame with 10. Bd2**
10. Bd2 defends against ...Nxc3, but blocks the queen's view of the d4-pawn. 10...Qxd4 continues the variation and the following are only moves: 11. Nxe4 Qxe4+ 12. Qe2 (protecting the knight on e4) 12...Bxd2 13. Kxd2 Qd5+ and the king usually moves to the queenside with 14. Kc2. White will soon win back the c4-pawn and in the resulting position Black has three pawns for the piece. From this position, the game is generally decided by the endgame. Black has to prove that their three pawns are more valuable in this endgame than White's bishop, but the records show this position to generally be favourable for White. …

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.text:
White castles their king to safety to unpin the knight and to start preparing e4.
Black can now choose to either play 8...Nbd7 or 8...O-O. Play is very likely to transpose, but different deviations from the main line are possible depending on which move Black plays first. The main difference is that after 8...O-O, Black has many possibilities of fully preventing e4, while after 8...Nbd7 trying to do so is more dangerous for Black.
In both positions, White is likely to play Qe2, preparing e4. There is, however, another option.

**Chasing the bishop**
It is not uncommon for White to play an early Nh4, chasing away the bishop. This option is most effective if White hasn't played 9. Qe2 yet, so that Qc2 can be played while gaining a tempo on the pawn.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/P.text:
8. Qc2
White activates the queen, who points towards the black kingside. Black develops with 8...Nc6

r1bqkb1r/p2n1ppp/2p1pn2/1p6/3P4/2NBPN2/P.text:
White returns the bishop to its original position, from where it supports the e4 pawn push. This is considered to be the main line.
The classical response by Black is 8...a6, protecting the b4-pawn in order to be able to free the light-squared bishop with c5 later. This does allow White to take control of the center with the immediate 9. e4, after which some very complicated positions can arise.
A slightly more modern and nowadays more popular response is 8...Bb7, the Wade variation. This makes the immediate 9. e4 less desirable for White, who usually responds by castling kingside immediately.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/1Bp5/3PP3/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
This check is an attempt to provoke concessions by Black who has three options now. Clearly the main move is 8...Nc6, which develops the knight on its best square but allows complications after 9.d5.
8...Bd7 9.Be2 leads to a slightly better position for White who profits from the fact that the pressure on d4 has been reduced for the moment.
8...Nd7 places the knight on a passive square. There will be no serious pressure against d4 now, and White should have the better chances thanks to his pawn centre.

**8.Bb5+**
This check is fine since Black cannot block with ...c6, and thus should play Nd7. If Black wants a dull, equal position with no dynamic energy, he can play Bd7. Black is fine here.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p2n2/4pb2/P1NP4/2N3P1/1.text:
Black finally pushes the e pawn forward, releasing the dark-squared bishop and fighting for the center.
If White ignores the pawn and prepares to castle with 9. Bg2, Black can start building pressure with 9...Rd8, aiming at White's queen, and 10...Be6 pressuring the knight (if 9...O-O-O then 10. a5! followed by 11. Qa4 starts a nasty attack on the queenside).
Therefore, White's best option is 9. dxe5, exchanging pawns in the center.

**History**
The Carlsbad variation is likely named after the tournament with the move's first appearance, that being the Karlsbad tournament from 1929. It was featured in a game between Capablanca and Vidmar.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.text:
White chooses to develop their knight instead of castling. This move prevents White's knight from jumping to e5 and chasing away the bishop.
White does still have the option of 9. Nh4, transposing into the Bled attack and claiming the bishop pair.
More common, however, is 9. Qe2, preparing e4 and going into the main line.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.text:
Black quickly castles their king to safety. This gives Black the option of playing 9...Bg6, which prevents 10. e4 and results in positions where White doesn't get as much central control.
White's main option is still 9. Qe2, threatening to play 10. e4.
White can also opt for 9. Nh4, transposing into the Bled attack.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2.text:
8...Nc6
Black simply develops. White continues with 9. a3, an important move to control b4 and prepare b2-b4.

r1bqkb1r/3n1ppp/p1p1pn2/1p6/3P4/2NBPN2/P.text:
Black protects the b-pawn so they can play 9...c5 without blundering a pawn.
Foreseeing this plan, White should play actively and take over the center with 9. e4, preparing to open up the center with either 10. d5 or 10. e5 and opening up the dark-squared bishop.
Less provocative setups have been tried as well. At the amateur level 9. O-O is very popular, but this poses no problems for players with the black pieces at all, since they score quite well in this line.
Another move that is played often is 9. a4. White does better than after 9. O-O, but has lost quite a bit of initiative.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p2n2/4Pb2/P1N5/2N3P1/1P.text: White exchanges the pawns in the center. Black doesn't have many valid options other than 9...Nxe5, recapturing the pawn.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.text: White prepares to push e4. Unlike after 8...O-O, Black has no real way of preventing this. 9...O-O transposes to the main line, while 9...Bg6 still gives Black room for deviation.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.text:
White is threatening to play 10. e4 with a tempo on the bishop. If Black allows this, they will have to fend off White's king-side attack, which comes in very quickly.

**Black allows e4**
9...Nbd7 is considered to be the main line. Black allows White to play e4 and hopes to fend off White's attack. The knight can serve as a potential defender by repositioning to f8.

**Black prevents e4**
Black has many options for preventing e4. The most popular being 9...Bg6.
After 9...Bg6 Black prevents e4 tactically. By retreating the bishop, 10. e4? is no longer played with tempo and in response Black plays 10...Bxc3! 11. bxc3 Nxe4 ∓ and White doesn't have the option of preventing Black from castling with Ba3 because Black is already castled. Because e4 isn't made possible, White generally chooses to try and capture the bishop with 10. Ne5.
A more direct way to prevent e4 is by occupying the square with a piece instead: 9...Ne4  blocks White's pawn and initiates a trade of pieces: 10. Bd3 and 10. Nxe4 are common. Black does however need to be prepared for the rare 10. g4! the Sämisch variation, where White is able to quickly storm Black's king with pawns.
Another way for Black to achieve this goal is by 9...Bg4, pinning and potentially capturing the f3 knight which is protecting d4. If White continues with their plan they will quickly find themselves down a pawn after 10. e4? Bxf3 11. gxf3 Qxd4 ⩱.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/P1N1PN.text:
9. a3
This move is important to control the b4 square and support b2-b4. Black is forced to play 9...Qa5, which prevents b4 by pinning the a3 pawn to the rook and pins the c3 knight to the king. This also supports ...Nb4.

r1bqkb1r/3n1ppp/p1p1pn2/1p6/3PP3/2NB1N2/.text:
White strikes in the center, opening up the dark-squared bishop in the process.
Black's main move is 9...c5, looking to break up White's center immediately. This move is played in the vast majority of games, and is Black's best option to open up the light-squared bishop and fight for an advantage.
A very rare sideline is 9...b4, the Pirc variation. This is the only other move (according to chess engines) that doesn't give White a winning advantage, since it gains a tempo on White's knight.

r3kb1r/ppq2ppp/2p2n2/4nb2/P1N5/2N3P1/1P2.text:
The central pawns have been exchanged. White can, and should, play 10. Bf4, developing the bishop and pinning the knight on e5. This also justifies White's previous move 8. g3.
White's knight on c4 is hanging, so there isn't many alternatives. 10. Nxe5? doesn't develop any of White's pieces and allows Black to quickly catch up in development.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.text: Black prophylactically retreats the bishop so that 10. e4 doesn't come with tempo. This allows for Black to win a pawn at the cost of giving White a big initiative.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.text:
Black prevents e4 tactically. By retreating the bishop, 10. e4? is no longer played with tempo and in response Black plays 10...Bxc3! 11. bxc3 Nxe4 ∓.
Instead, White should chase Black's light-squared bishop with 10. Ne5.
Some players have played 10. Rd1?! in this position, since this move is played anyways. But this is inaccurate, because 10...Nbd7 now prevents the knight from jumping to e5 and trading off the bishop. While chess engines evaluate 10. Rd1 as approximately equal, Black outperforms White in practice.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2.text: This move develops the knight to it's most natural square, but also invites White to play 10. e4. This move also sets up Nb6, attacking the light-squared bishop and uncovering the black queen's attack on the d4-pawn. This tactic can cost White a pawn if they are not careful with their pawn-advance.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/q1bp4/2P2B2/P1N1PN.text:
9...Qa5
This move is forced, pinning the a3 pawn to the rook, preventing b2-b4 and supporting ...Nb4 ideas. White has a sideline and 2 mainline moves.
10. Nd2 is the sideline, avoiding the complications of the mainlines. As Nb3 is threatened, black responds with ...Be7.
The mainlines 10. Rd1 and 10. O-O-O are not for the faint of heart, as they lead to wild, extremely complicated positions.

r1bqkb1r/3n1ppp/p3pn2/1pp5/3PP3/2NB1N2/P.text:
Black strikes back at White's center, opening up the light-squared bishop.
This is the main branching point of the mainline Meran, since White has to choose between one of two pawn breaks: e5 and d5.
10. e5 is the Old variation.
10. d5 is Reynold's variation.

r3kb1r/ppq2ppp/2p2n2/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.text:
This move pins the knight on e5 to the black queen, which is its only defender at the moment. Moving the knight isn't an option, so the only move to add another defender is 10...Nfd7.
10...Bd6?? fails to defend the knight because it loses a piece. The d6 square is attacked by both the c4 knight and the queen on d1 and only defended by Black's queen on c7.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBPP3/2N2N2/1.text:
White takes up the full center. If Black simply plays 10...O-O we are once again following the main line.
One thing that sets this position apart from 8...O-O 9. Qe2 9...Bg6 is that White was actually able to play e4. Black can take the pawn but it is not free. 10...Bxc3 removes an important defender of e4. After 11. bxc3 Nxe4 12. Ba3! =/∞
Black is up a pawn, but White has prevented them from castling king-side. Black will have to castle queen-side, where White has the open b-file and the far-advanced a-pawn.
If Black gets greedy and tries to win more pawns with 12...Nxc3? White is quick to get the upper hand after 13. Qb2!, forking the knight and the pawn on b7.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBPP3/2N2N2.text:
White has been building up to this move for a while. This central expansion hits Black's light-squared bishop with tempo. Black has two squares to retreat the bishop to.
10...Bg6 lets the bishop keep an eye on the e4-pawn, which must now either be pushed to e5 or protected by White's bishop.
10...Bg4 immediately pins White's knight on f3, making the e5 pawn-break possible and also allowing various tactics revolving around the d4-pawn unless defended again.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p5/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1P.text: This move defends the pinned knight. White no longer has any moves to increase the pressure on the e5 knight, so play usually continues by developing the light-squared bishop with 11. Bg2.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBPP3/2N2N2/.text:
Black retreats the bishop, keeping an eye on e4. White must either protect or push the pawn.
11. Bd3 defends the pawn and threatens to trade off the light-squared bishops after 12. e5.
11. e5 immediately chases away the knight, but is likely to transpose to the lines with 11. Bd3.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p5/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1P.text:
White develops the light-squared bishop and prepares to castle short.
From this position, two moves have been played historically: f6 and g5.
11...f6 is the old mainline, defending the knight.
11...g5 is the most popular line nowadays and is considered the best move for Black.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/Pb1PP3/2NB1N2.text: 11...Bh5 sidesteps the discovered attack and pins the f3 knight.

r3kb1r/ppqn1p1p/2p5/4nbp1/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.text:
11...g5 is the most popular line nowadays and is considered the best move for Black. Because the kingside pawn structure is significantly weakened, Black will usually resort to castling queenside.
12. Bxg5?? would blunder 12...Nxc4. The bishop can't stay on the same diagonal as the black queen, so some pieces have to be traded.
12. Bxe5 allows Black to secure the bishop pair after 12...Nxe5 but White gets compensation after 13. Qd4 f6 14. O-O-O preventing Black from castling queenside.
12. Ne3 is played most often, planning to take the light-squared bishop. After 12...gxf4 13. Nxf5 O-O-O 14. Qc2 Black has two isolated pawns on the kingside, but a four on two majority on the queenside and has control of the d-file. White should soon castle short.

**History**
The Morozevich is named after the player Alexander Morozevich, who was the first person to play the variation and did so against Garry Kasparov in the year 2000.

r3kb1r/ppqn2pp/2p2p2/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.text:
This is the old mainline. Black protects the knight with a pawn in order to protect the knight.
The usual continuation after f6 is 12. O-O Nc5 13. Ne3 Bg6 14. b4.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/7b/Pb1PP3/2NB1N2.text: White can finally go through with their plan of taking over the center with 12. e5.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/4P2b/Pb1P4/2NB1N.text:
White finally takes over the centre, with tempo on Black's knight.
Black's main response is 12...Nd5, trying to trade it off for White's c3 knight. Nearly all games continue 13. Nxd5 cxd5 14. Qe3. White unpins their knight and prepares Ng5 to start an attack on Black's king-side. Black has a few possible responses.
14...Be7 defends the g5-square immediately. White can however still go for 15. Ng5, initiating a trade of minor pieces and queens 15...Bxg5 16. Qxg5 Qxg5 17. Bxg5⩲, after which Black re-positions the knight to c6 through b8. White's advantage lies mostly in the bishop pair and the advanced pawns.
Apart from 15. Ng5, White can keep the pieces on the board with 15. Bd2, after which Black usually executes the previously mentioned knight manoeuvre. There is many more ideas for both sides which I recommend exploring through the lichess openings database.

14...Re8 is a more modest move, making place for the knight to defend h7. White can choose to tactically trade off pieces with 15. Ng5 Nf8 16. Nxh7!? Nxh7 18. Bxh7 Kxh7 19. Qh3 g6 20. g4 =
14...Bg6 15. Bxg6 fxg6!? trades off the light-squared bishops and opens up the f8 rook. However, after 16. Ng5 Black has to defend their pawn with 16...Re8 not only to defend the pawn, but also to free the f8 square for the knight for if White were to play 17. Qh3, threatening Qxh7 and attacking the e6 pawn.
